utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remind you what we agreed upon yesterday. Mr. Kovacic will start to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Maric, and it will last for some 20 minutes. After that, the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, will start to cross-examine, and we have in mind the fact that after the pause, at 1.00, we will be back here at 2.30, hoping to have completed with this witness by 4.00 so that the witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric. We have met before. My name is Kovacic, I represent the Defence of Mr. Cerkez. And since you are here, I should like to seize this opportunity and ask you certain things, because you might know them and perhaps you will help us explain some matters. In view of the office that you held, that you told us about, in the municipality of Busovaca, you are presumably familiar with the organisation of power in your municipality, and you told us about that. But did you know -- did you have any at least rudimentary knowledge as to what was going on in the municipality surrounding Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the neighbouring municipalities, yes, I was aware of the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So tell us, do you remember if in Vitez there was also a coalition HDZ-SDA after the elections, the only difference being that the Serb side, or rather the party of the Serbs, was not a member of the coalition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that these three ruling parties, if I may call them that, were the strongest in the municipality of Vitez too, except that the SDS was not a member of the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as a result of the elections, Muslims and Croats shared the power in Vitez too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mayor was Mr. Ivica Santic, and as far as I can recall, the president of the executive board, that is, the government, was Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just for the sake of other people, we understand it, but Ivica Santic is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Croat, and Fuad Kaknjo is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, another matter regarding the situation in the neighbouring municipality. The chief body, which protagonised the defence, the organisation of the defence against the JNA aggression in 1992, the municipal body, that is, was the so-called HVO Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You in Busovaca also had such a staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And so did Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps who headed that body in the municipality of Vitez, who was the commander or the chairman or what of that staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chairman, the president of the HVO, was Mr. Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of the government, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the government, and the staff itself, which began to operate before the government was founded, before the HVO, if that is what you mean. The president of the assembly, the mayor, was Ivan Santic. And Mr. Marijan Skopljak, I think, was responsible for the executive branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Marijan Skopljak held that position even when the defence department was set up, that is, when the government was set up and the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. To the best of my recollection, he headed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Mario Cerkez at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mario Cerkez in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the latter half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Latter half of 1993, you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what kind of office did he hold in 1992, say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what was his position in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He commanded the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't know the exact date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one subject more. In the organisation of government, even the former Yugoslavia, which was then taken over by the Republic of Bosnia and even by the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the municipalities had what in the former Yugoslavia was called People's Defence secretariats. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that system, that make-up, was also taken over in the ensuing period. You just mentioned defence offices.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that these defence offices, or former secretariats, were responsible for the preparation and the organisation of civilian support to the military Defence organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could one say that essentially all defence matters in the municipality fell within the jurisdiction of those civilian bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All preparations went through the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So what does preparation mean, actually?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, lists of reservists. Well, the mobilisation, the compilation of lists, based on the former wartime orders, for instance, in the former, that is, JNA. If somebody was an infantry man in the former system, then he would again be an infantry man in the defence office, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the defence office had a record of all the individuals, depending on -- classified according to the rank or the type of the service that somebody did in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who was paying for those troops?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those people were paid by the government, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But all the technical matters relating to it were done by the defence office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the technical preparations were conducted by the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us take a simple example. When the defence office summons a particular person, that is, finds him on the records, that is the man they need, called him, established that he is safe and alive, that he has not lost a leg meanwhile or something happened to him, and sends him to a unit, and this is where the job of the defence office ends?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as of that moment, it is the unit which is responsible for that individual?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit which took up that man is responsible for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one question more about this. You showed us when you went through documents that the central administration, that is, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for all intents and purposes, did not function. Would you agree that the same held true of the organisation of the People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is why the municipalities undertook to deal with more defence matters than they would otherwise do.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the complete -- when the entire central administration or central government of Sarajevo was completely blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in the organisation of power in the former Yugoslavia, municipalities constituted an important element in the organisation of power; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In fact, when the system fell apart in Bosnia in 1992, the municipalities assumed all the power prerogatives.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was only the municipality which could accept it and lead the people during all those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, just one question more. Can you tell us, please, if you have ever, ever seen Mr. Cerkez in the municipality in Busovaca, I mean, the building, the municipal hall, ever coming for any official visit, meeting, session?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Busovaca anywhere, any place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when did you first have contact with Mr. Kordic's lawyers, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was your summary first drafted, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summary was written when I arrived here on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was it first drafted, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 28th of May was last -- I can't remember now. This week, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sunday. Sunday. It was Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was all drafted and translated on the Sunday, was it, or the Sunday and the Monday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived on Thursday, and on Sunday I prepared this summary for signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you first met the lawyers for Mr. Kordic, where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you meet them in any other place since then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents that you've produced, who selected them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents, I saw them here. I did not see them before because my whole archive, when I left the municipality of Busovaca, stayed behind in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who selected the documents, then, that have been produced to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents, well, they -- here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the position that so far as you know the entire Busovaca archive still exists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Busovaca in 1994. Whether it still exists or whether it does not exist, I cannot really say because for the past six years I've ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These documents, you see, that have been produced to us are all sequentially numbered from 1992 through to one document or a couple of documents in 1993, and they all have a very similar heading to them; not all identical but similar. Do these appear to be originals that have been copied from the archives, or what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are originals from the archive -- copies of the originals from the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had access to the archive in order to make this selection, please? You must know; it must have been explained to you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I was with these gentlemen a year and a half ago, and I arrived here, and as for these documents, I don't know who did it because I don't know. But they are my documents, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One notices that there is no official letterhead in 1992 and that the letterhead has simply been typed on in all cases. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true at all, what you are saying. These are originals which were written on the day for which these documents were written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The letterhead has been typed on; it hasn't got a printed or a formal appearance to it, save in the case of one of the documents which, I think, is number 262/1, for the 11th of November, where there is a formal title page. Were you just typing on the headings of these documents in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were typing headings, and we also had the letterhead forms which were done by the HVO with its full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any particular reason for not using the letterhead forms on nearly all of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times we used one type; at other times we used the other type. But as a rule we used the typed ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are there any other documents that you've been able to refer to before coming to give evidence here, like a diary, if you have one, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never kept a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other documents that you've been able to refer to help you give evidence here today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in the territory of my municipality have stuck in my memory, it is all imprinted on my mind, so that is how I could speak about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the overall reality that you're describing for the Judges that the Croats in Busovaca were totally blameless at all times? Is that what you're describing for us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to portray the situation as it was in Busovaca. Nobody is infallible. Everybody has mistakes; everybody errs. And there were murders and all sorts of things, and nobody denies that all those things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have the full strength from you, please, of how bad the HVO and the Croats were. Murders and all that sort of thing, shall we start with those? What murders in the period 1992/1993 are inexcusable but attributed to the HVO, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. Tell us about, enumerate, the murders in 1992 and 1993 that are inexcusable and that are attributed to the HVO or the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murders, to begin with, any perpetrator of a murder should be punished regardless of who or what he is. But what was done by extremists, that is, what I would call people who committed misdeeds which are attributed to the HVO, I condemned the incidents; the incident when Mr. Ibrahim Hodzic was murdered, Mirsad Delija, and those horrendous things that happened in Ahmici. You should also know that I condemn also that which Muslim units did to Croats, because 2.700 men, Croats, died in these lands. Every life is significant for man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's focus, then, on the things you've told us about. Who murdered Ibrahim Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrahim Hodzic, the investigation was under way. As far as I know, it was a policeman, a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember because the investigation was under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this was a military policeman killing in the course of work for the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that he killed. The problem has to be approached from a different angle. There were such things happening. If somebody lost a brother, a father, then the hatred in him grows towards everybody. And the individual who commits such a crime must be punished, must be called to account, regardless of who or what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps you'd like to tell us who murdered Mirsad Delija and why.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said these investigations were under way. The reports were not yet final while I was still in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the territory of Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Busovaca, it is that part while I was in the government practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until? Until when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1994, are you saying that this report into Mirsad Delija's death was never taken to any form of conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation was being conducted and the investigators were doing their job. I did not receive it, the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Presumably, and assuming that the archive of the HVO is complete, the archive from which these documents are taken, the report on Mirsad Delija's death will be in the archive, won't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation was conducted by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the report would still have gone to the HVO, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get it, and therefore I cannot speak about what I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please help me. Would the report of the police into the death of Mirsad Delija have gone to the HVO and be in its archive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the way it should be, but it did not arrive while I was there in 1994. The investigation was under way and I cannot tell you exactly because I did not get the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Knowing that you were coming here to give evidence, you didn't ask to see that document, and nobody showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn, then, to Ahmici, since you mentioned it. Who committed the appalling crimes of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I learned, there was heavy fighting there, and I cannot say who committed that because this was another municipality and I was not present there. But I condemn every crime, especially the one committed in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You were mayor of a town, just tell us again, how many kilometres from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town is about 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few minutes in a car; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in all the time since then, with all your seniority in office, you can't tell these Judges who committed -- I'm just looking for the terms you used -- those horrendous things that happened in Ahmici? Can you not tell us, please, who did it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say, because I wasn't present. There was also fierce fighting in the territory of Busovaca municipality. You have to know that we were non-stop shelled in Busovaca. We were attacked by almost 20.000 people, and we were defending ourselves. The ratio was 10:1. That was terrible. You couldn't move freely so that you could come and see. Everybody was dealing with their own problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That doesn't stop your receiving information, then or thereafter, about this atrocity. Please tell me, or tell the Judges: Are you saying you have at no time learnt anything about who were the perpetrators of these horrendous crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't there at that time, and I don't know what happened, but I heard that that day was terrible, that a lot of people were killed, both civilian and military. I cannot tell you what I don't know. I took an oath here to tell the truth, and I want to say the truth, because I experienced this truth personally. I know what it was like to be there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These questions started with my asking you if the Croats were blameless, and you were to tell us in what way they weren't blameless. So far you've been unable to name, I think, any murderer or any perpetrator of a crime. Tell me this: When you learnt of the arrest of Blaskic and the later surrender by himself or by the State of Croatia of Kordic, did you think these men had been wrongly charged, from all you knew of them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know about these people, Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, Mr. Dario Kordic, and Mr. Cerkez, I know that these are innocent men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the mayor of Busovaca at the critical time, you were the holder of detailed and relevant information, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was leading the civilian affairs during the war and I was getting exclusively civilian orders; that is, I issued orders in respect of civilian affairs. And the military units and military commanders conducted the military affairs, and those were in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, on one answer you say that these men are innocent, to your knowledge, and the next answer you try to distinguish between civilian and military affairs. My question to you was quite particular: Are you and were you the holder of detailed and relevant information about what was happening that led these two men to trial in this institution? Your answer is yes, isn't it; you had and have a lot of relevant information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to say this: A man who commits something wrong, who commits an evil, is a criminal. A person of whom no such thing was proved cannot be considered a criminal. I know a little bit about law, because I was involved in it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just help us with this: Did it ever occur to you, with your position of central knowledge, to offer to help the Office of the Prosecutor with what your knowledge was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the documents remained in the archives. They were accessible. I left in 1994; I left the municipality, that is, and I cannot speak to the whereabouts of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer to my question is: No, it never occurred to you to get in touch with the Prosecutor here and say, "Well, I actually know what happened. Let me come and help you and tell you," did it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came today and I want to present the events which occurred in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who replaced you as mayor, and when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, when? What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, did you hear the question which you were asked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the question, but I did not quite understand what the gentleman was driving at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was the following: You left Busovaca in 1994. Who replaced you as mayor, and when? You either know, and then you'll answer. In case you don't know or you've forgotten, this is not really here something where we should exercise our memories here; you should simply declare that you don't know. But the question was very simple and clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just had not understood what the gentleman was asking me. But I do know. Mr. Glavocevic replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And he then remained mayor until when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained mayor until -- I know that he was replaced by Mr. Niko Grubesic, and then he in turn was replaced by Nikica Petrovic, who was the mayor until a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Maric, did you come back to Busovaca since 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did come to Busovaca. I was heading the office of the Central Bosnia canton for forestry and agriculture till 1996, and then after that the Central Bosnia HDZ cantonal office, and now I am officially the president of the parliament of the Central Bosnia canton. So these are the duties that I have held since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you live currently in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reside in Busovaca with my family, and every day I commute to Travnik, where my office is. And I have to say that Travnik has become a very Muslim town, because a lot of Croats have been expelled from there. And at first it was very difficult, but I have managed to successfully discharge my duties there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you maintained contact with those mayors who have come after you, Mr. Grubesic and Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any policy expressed by one of those mayors to potential Prosecution witnesses in this case, discouraging at least one of them from coming to give evidence here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me turn to some generalities. But before I do, there's no aspect of Busovaca life and there's no part of Busovaca territory that was kept from you at the material time, was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know that Busovaca, with all its territory, which was populated by Croats, Bosniak Muslims and the Serbs, was one integral territory; however, through attacks and warfare, the territory has been split up. And now we're engaging in building up the Federation, so now we're looking at it as one unit and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll cut you short, because we have limited time. At the material time, that is, 1992, 1993, possibly 1994, there was no aspect of Busovaca life or Busovaca territory that was kept from you; you were free to travel everywhere, you met everyone, you were able to get to know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was it possible, when during the conflict a Croat could not come to the area controlled by the ABiH? You couldn't leave the territory of Busovaca municipality, that is, the area controlled -- the area of town controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to press on with this. I'm going to ask you about various people and ask whether you or they should know more about Mr. Kordic and his involvement at the time. Should you know as much as or more than Milorad Jovic of what Mr. Kordic was doing? Who should know more about Mr. Kordic, you or Milorad Jovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know, Milorad Jovic is a Serb. Regardless of whether he's a Serb or a Muslim or a Croat in Busovaca, whoever talked to Mr. Kordic knew him, knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the other names are these: Nikica Petrovic, Milenko Bilanovic, Anto Stipac, and the man Hodzic, who was vice-president of the HDZ ABiH. Now, as between you and those men, who should know Kordic better or best? You?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone knew Kordic, knew him from the school days. And we socialised. When we started up the party, we were together. We had contacts non-stop, so I know Kordic as a good person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard that before, and I'll come back to it, in which case I'll move on, because I want to save time. If you can't answer the question, I'll move on. Mr. Kordic's job before all this developed was actually rather a modest one, wasn't he? He ran the newspaper for the business and was a publicity person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first he worked as a journalist for the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he was a keen member of the league of communists at his factory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of -- it was open to anyone who wanted to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please answer the question. He was a keen and active member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I never was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the new party was formed, there was obviously an opportunity for ambitious people. Kordic's father was ambitious for him, wasn't he, Pero Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody had a right to form a party if they wanted to, whether they were ambitious or not. That depended on what they wanted to do. Perhaps I was more ambitious. That is a matter of judgement. If you do not value yourself, how are you going to be able to value anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would help me if you'd answer the question. Kordic was ambitious and his father was ambitious for him too, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any person who joined the party had an ambition. Everybody was trying to see a reflection of himself in a leader who would lead the party well, who would show the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look ahead, confirm this if it's right: In due course that party established, without any involvement of the Muslims, a government called the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Muslims were also part of the HVO government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The establishment of the HVO was without election, without referendum; it was simply an imposition; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A referendum was not necessary. Through the referendum we achieved an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. We achieved that, thank God, on the 1st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO was created by a political party and it was imposed on an area without referendum, without election; true or false?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A referendum was not necessary. We were involved in a struggle to preserve the identity of a people. This happened after the attacks of the JNA against the Slovenia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, the question, once again, is a very simple one. What you call the HVO is not something which was the result of an election; those people were simply not elected. That was the question. Please answer with yes or no; there is no reason for you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no referendum; that is true. There was no referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that your area fell under the government of something that had been created by a single political party; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can state is that it is true that it was created by the Croat Democratic Union, which was the leading party representing the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it received support of over 90 per cent of the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The experience of communist states, and of your state as well, was that once a body, political or military, has power and exercises it, it's very difficult to take it away, what you all discovered through decades of Tito's leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This period after 1990, when a new society was formed, when the new parliaments were established, this is something completely different from the Titoist regime which was in power until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the new system. I'm asking you about the experience of communist states; namely, that once you take power, if you take it with sufficient firmness, it's very difficult to have it taken away from you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know that everyone wants to win the elections and then keep the power. That is the goal of every party, to rule as long as possible, and it is up to the population to support it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened here -- and I'm just looking at things overall before I come to matters of detail -- is that the party's ambition grew and with it, Mr. Kordic's ambition; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just Kordic's ambition. The ambitions of every member of the party grew. Everyone wanted that his party grew and prospered in a democratic way, along the democratic principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we're going to see as we review the history is Mr. Kordic first in civilian clothes, then in civilian clothes with a firearm, and then in uniform, and that parallels the development of your party and the government going from being a party to a government and to a government operating by force; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's not like you're saying. You should know the circumstances and the events that were taking place from 1990 onward. Events kept succeeding each other, and very quickly the war and the refugees, and you had to defend your home. There were a host of problems. Every man in those territories wanted to preserve their homes. We defended ourselves; we did not attack anyone. If you had spent only one minute there, you would have experienced the same stress and the same pain, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must stop you because we don't have time --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we have hundreds of people who are sick from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the end of the period with which we are particularly concerned, had Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic started to fall out, to your and everybody else's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any quarrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that in the latter part of the period with which we are concerned, or even in the middle part, Mr. Kordic was taking military decisions and authority, to the damage of the population it may be, but he was taking them, and that this was causing difficulties as between him and Blaskic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. Mr. Dario Kordic was a politician and he was a politician throughout, and Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was the chief of staff and he conducted the military matters. And the Main Staff was in Mostar, under the command of General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that topic later in its sequence. But you're maintaining, as I think you are from your answers, that your party was essentially democratic in some way. Tell us, please, why Mr. Cicak was so unacceptable to the party, when all he was voicing was democratic opinions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat Democratic Union is a democratic party. Mr. Dragutin Cicak, who was for a period of time the vice-president of the party in Busovaca, was a man who came from Zenica -- so he was not a local man from Busovaca; he only had a weekend home in Busovaca -- but this is a man who, due to mental illness, took an early retirement. He had good and bad sides like any other person who may have good or bad sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You and, if I may say so, you'll be helped to know, all the other Defence witnesses are now referring to his mental illness. Tell me, please, when it first seemed to you important to mention this man's mental illness as in some way significant.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He often complained of being ill, and when he was supposed to come up with certain programmes he often said, "I just cannot do this because I have problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He resigned on the 7th of April of 1991 -- the document is 2732; I'm not going to take us through it for the moment for want of time -- but that wasn't the end of his involvement in these matters, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the documents to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 2732, if we could make that available. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. Mr. Maric, you told us that Mr. Cicak was suffering from mental illness.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you assume that he had a mental illness rather than another type of illness? You say that he was tired; he could have had any physical illness. Why do you speak of a mental illness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Mr. Dragutin Cicak told me personally that he had such an illness. Personally we were good friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You wanted to have a look at the document. It's coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we put on the ELMO the second sheet in English -- sorry, the third sheet of that document, which begins, "I have neither the will nor the strength to fight against the fools ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with this point quickly, it's true, isn't it, that in his resignation he identified Ivan Pervan as somebody he couldn't work with and maintained right at that early stage that he was being supported by Kordic, although Kordic was somebody he was prepared to discuss with in public; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct, because if you can tell a priest that he's crazy, that he's not all there, then I think it speaks for itself. A man who is a priest for more than 6.000 men, a man who has been helping people all along, to say something like that to such a priest, I think it shows quite clearly what kind of a man that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question but we don't have enough time to go into questions twice. So if you don't answer the first time, then I'm going to move on. On the 13th of August, in Busovaca, your party of 1991 was already calling the man Kljuic to account, a senior and influential politician. Was that because he was a democrat by instinct and you didn't like his contrary views?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You ought to know that Mr. Stjepan Kljuic, as the president of the HDZ, never came to Busovaca. And he was married -- of course, his personal thing -- to a Muslim from Busovaca, and she also had some relatives there. He would go to other places but he never came to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, no doubt, was his decision. But your local party, ambitious for power, was summoning Kljuic and calling him to account as soon after its creation as August of 1991. This is all a reflection of local ambition, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a reflection -- it is not a reflection of local ambition. But if a president is to lead a people, then he must do it honestly and fairly rather than leave that people to be destroyed by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Things progressed, and we know that on the 4th of November of 1991, you can see the document if you want to, there was a meeting of the Travnik regional community, with people attending, I think, including Cicak. On that occasion a confidential memo was sent to Tudjman -- we don't have the memo, I don't think -- or reference was made to such a memo that had been sent in October. You all swore yourselves to secrecy or declared yourselves to secrecy over the memo. What was the memo about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see it, if possible, to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Z20. Now, we can see that you were attending, and under number 2 of the conclusions, which can go on the ELMO, please, conclusion number 2: Confidential conclusion of the 22nd of October, sent to Dr. Franjo Tudjman, unanimously supported by members of the Croatian Regional Community of Travnik, promising to respect the secrecy of this information. What was it about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I was at a meeting, which is shown here. It is quite true that the conclusion is supported unanimously on the 22nd of October, 1991, which is sent to the president of the HDZ. But you should know that the Croat Democratic Union is a party of every Croat, regardless of where he lives, be it in Canada, Australia, Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, I would ask you to answer the questions that you are being asked, in order to be able to finish -- complete your cross-examination within the time limit; otherwise you will have to come back here on Monday. We really have a schedule. What can you tell us precisely about the documents addressed to President Tudjman? Please answer the question. And all the rest about what was the HDZ, we know; we've been informed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this document sent to Dr. Franjo Tudjman, it was said that the Croat Democratic Union would respect the democratic principles in the rest of Croats and all other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That hardly requires secrecy. I would have thought public acclamation might be more appropriate. Wouldn't that be the case? Why secrecy, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is specified here that the secrecy, it is simply the code secret, because the majority of documents were strictly confidential; that is, that was the marking taken over from the old system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know that Croatia, via Dr. Franjo Tudjman, assisted, and significantly, in the conduct of the war, including the war in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia was helping Bosnia-Herzegovina, helping equally the Croat and the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time of the fighting between the Croats and the Bosnians, are you suggesting that Dr. Franjo Tudjman was helping the Bosnians at that stage, or was he just helping the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was helping them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what help was he giving to the Bosnians that they might, what, that they might do something to the Croats? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was helping both the Croats and the Muslims with food, other supplies, and all that was necessary to survive in these territories. He received over 500 displaced persons. There is hardly any other state which received so many people as Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, under these circumstances, if you are telling us that Mr. Tudjman was supporting the Bosnians and the Croats, what were the objectives and the motivations of Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The motives of Mr. Tudjman were that Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an autonomous state, is within its borders, because Croatia was the first one to recognise Bosnia after its independence, which was acquired in a referendum on the 1st of March, when the Croats and the Muslims and a part of loyal Serbs voted for its independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Maric. I'm speaking about the time period where the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims started, which means from 1993 onwards, from January 1993 onwards. Did Mr. Tudjman continue to support Croats and Muslims, the two parties which were opposing one another?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tudjman was supporting them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that Tudjman was sending arms to both sides, or military personnel to both sides?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, weapons were arriving in the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina invariably through Croatia, because the only roads that took one to Bosnia-Herzegovina were across Croatia, whether it arrived legally or, as some call it, illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know -- it's a simple question, and I'll make it simpler -- was Tudjman providing arms to the Muslims to use against the Croats; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman never said that the Croats and the Muslims should have a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the question you were asked. The question that you were asked is: Did Mr. Tudjman send arms to Muslims for the Croats? Please answer by saying "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether it was being sent or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he certainly sent arms to the Croats, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody was trying to manage. Even Saudi Arabia was sending arms to the Muslims side, and the Croats did not get them. Instead of food, they were getting ammunition in tins. There are documents about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Maric, to save time. You have another chance to answer the question, please. Tudjman sent arms to the Croats; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes he did, sometimes he did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because he was in a very difficult situation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you know perfectly well some of Tudjman's thinking, don't you, because you went to meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know what other people think, but I was present at meetings when Mr. Tudjman said, in so many words, that we were fighting democratically, and he never mentioned that we were fighting against the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many meetings with Tudjman did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six meetings all in all, as far as I can remember at the moment, that is, since the party was formed until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many meetings did you go to with Tudjman in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 I did not go.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993 I was present at one, and at the time when there was a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was in March of 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About a month before Ahmici. What was the purpose of that discussion, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can already assume that it did not initiate the conflict. We went to talk to President Tudjman about the cessation of any further activities regarding conflicts in the territory of Central Bosnia, to come and talk to President Alija to withdraw his extremists who had initiated those problems, to avoid conflicts, because President Tudjman was an authority and he could talk to presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go to take his instructions on how to conduct yourselves in the coming months?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go to get instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that amongst the means by which arms were brought to Busovaca from Tudjman was Bruno Susnjar, who regularly collected arms; would that be correct? We've heard evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly if he was the one who brought arms. I know that arms were arriving, that some individuals brought arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anto Sliskovic, did he bring them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, who did? We've heard those two names mentioned, but you tell us. You were there. Who brought the arms from Tudjman? There's also the man Franjo Kristo, a police chief. But never mind. You tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly all the people who brought arms. All I know is that arms arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you're now not able to remember, that it's some form of amnesia, or that you never really knew? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the people who brought them. I know that arms arrived in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have to remember them all. Can you just help us with one name of somebody who brought arms from Tudjman to Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, Tudjman did not bring them, because arms were arriving through Croatia, because arms arriving, as I said, were arriving through Croatia. Whether it was brought in another country, in other states, I do not know that and I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kordic had been elected to a job in defence. Why defence? What skills did he have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for when the government was formed, then, in 1990, Mr. Kordic -- and the regulations, the conditions, the qualifications that had to be met to hold that office were met by Mr. Kordic. What it required was to have somebody with a university degree, and he had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But no special qualifications for defence of any kind; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do not need any special education for that, to be able to head such an office, because he had under him individuals who were responsible for individual departments in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th of November of 1991, last event before we move to 1992, there was a meeting in Grude, and the result of that was that Kordic became a vice-president; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you told us this: Senior representatives of various municipalities in which the Croats lived formed the presidency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't hear the interpretation of the first half of the sentence. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I was quoting from paragraph 14 of your summary, if my notes are correct, and what you said in paragraph 14 of your summary was: "The senior representatives of the various municipalities in which Croats lived formed the presidency of the HZ HB, which became a legislative body." Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite. Yes, that is right. For instance, I, as a municipal mayor -- if a Croat was a municipal mayor, then he joined that presidency, and presidents of the executive board were the second position. For instance, in our case it was a Muslim, Asim Sunulahpasic. There were many municipalities where that was not the case and where Croats also were the heads of local governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so Kordic, but correct me if I've got this wrong, Kordic becomes the vice-president with an interest in a particular area; is that about right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean, with a particular responsibility? I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you, really, built on what you said in your statement. "The senior representatives of the various municipalities formed the presidency." So it looks as though the composition of the presidency is municipality-based, and therefore the representatives on the presidency may represent bits of the area, bits of the municipalities. Kordic became a vice-president. Was that to reflect his interest in a particular part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kordic was elected vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, help me with this: In the local area, who was the senior politician if it wasn't Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, Mr. Kordic was a vice-president. The 18th of November, 1991 is when the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded, and that was that umbrella organisation and he became its vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your area, Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- was there any politician of the party senior to Kordic, or was he really the local man? Was he the local political --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He continued to be president of the Busovaca HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's still not an answer to the question. Was he -- go on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Busovaca HDZ, I was the mayor of the municipality, and so in that hierarchy we were practically on a par, because the presidency consisted of all the representatives of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See, when we come to the fighting and the war, the question we're going to want your help with is who was controlling the military? Do you understand? Who was actually running the war? I want to know, and I'll give you advance notice so that you can think about it, what politician other than Kordic had the seniority in your local area to command the soldiers? Would you like to deal with it now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to answer. The presidency of the HZ HB, headed by President Boban. He was the pivotal figure, President Mate Boban, a master of sciences. During wartime operations, the president of the HZ HB, that is, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, was Master Boban, master of arts, and he was the commander in chief, the head of everything. The government which was established later was headed by Prime Minister Jadranko Prlic, and it had its ministries. I explained it to you yesterday when I testified that the army was run by Milivoje Petkovic, who was hierarchically -- and he hierarchically followed the chain of command downward by military districts; and in Central Bosnia it was Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, and then again in the descending order to brigade commanders. That was the hierarchy which was set up. The government -- you are confusing governments. The HVO government acted as the civilian wing and the HVO, secondly, the military component, it is responsible for activities having to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, if you think that this would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to adjourn for half an hour and we will start again at half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on to 1992, I'm going back to the question that you were answering at length before we broke, and I want a single, if it's possible, name in answer to this question: In the war, what was the name of the politician who affected any measure of control over the military in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the name of the politician?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the military affairs were handled by the headquarters of Petkovic, down to Blaskic, and of the civilians, it was Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What about Mr. Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dario Kordic was only a politician, just like I was just a politician of the civilian HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to give you one more chance. Let me explain it to you in simple terms. In the last big war, it might have been said that Churchill, or on the other side Hitler, commanded the war but in each case was a politician. Now, who was the politician who commanded the war in your territory, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina the main politician was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, when you were cut off, who was the politician?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all politicians, and he was our politician, Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. So he was the leading politician. Was he the one who was communicating instructions to the military, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He communicated with everyone, regardless of whether they were the military or civilian, because he advocated the peace in the area; he talked with the UNPROFOR representatives, with anyone who expressed the desire to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 16th of January of 1992, you were at the Busovaca Cultural Club, where there was the rally. If it's absolutely necessary, you can be shown it again. It's a video. But we've seen it enough times and we're pressed for time. Do you remember the rally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you think that the observations Kordic made linking the fate of your part of the territory to Germany, and to the hope, were neutral statements, or do you think they had any potentially unsatisfactory significance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Kordic -- and I was present there -- he did not irritate anyone with his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about Kostroman? And I can just tell, you as a matter of interest, that you're seen on the tape -- as the camera pans around, you're seen on the tape in the middle of Kostroman's speech. What did you think of Kostroman's speech, where he was saying that this was Croatian land and that Croatian laws would be enforced there? What did you think of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone has the right to say whatever they want. However, for me and those who were present there, this was not acceptable. I'm a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is my country. And I also respect the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it surprise you to know that a Muslim witness testified that this speech aroused associations with the fascist state of Croatia during World War II and proved to be extremely troubling to them, that is, to the Muslims? Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that speech is concerned, as I said, everyone has the right to say whatever they want, and people can accept or not accept the speech of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're a local resident, you know your Muslims. The question was quite simple. Does it surprise you that that speech should arouse those sort of concerns in your fellow inhabitant Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone could be concerned, whether it is an irritating type of statement or something else. It depends on how people take it. And as far as the Kostroman statement is concerned, everybody is responsible for their own speeches and their own actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you won't answer the question, will you answer this: Did you at any stage disassociate yourself from Kostroman's speech and from his stance on basically trying to join up this part of the territory with Croatia? Did you at any stage do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a view of Mr. Kostroman. My views are completely different. I respect the Croatian state, but I also respect my own state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I am a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I protect the interests of the people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, that is all very well, and I believe Mr. Nice could move on to another question, because the witness has answered after his own fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept that at about this time, that's the beginning of January of 1992, Mr. Kordic, who in the rally was in plain clothes, that is, in civilian clothes, do you accept that about this time he also was seen with a firearm, a pistol, on the occasion of the stopping of the convoy, called the Banana Convoy, at Kaonik on the 17th of January?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general, do you accept that he moved from being a person in plain clothes through to being an authoritative figure carrying a firearm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Mr. Kordic carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for reference purposes, that was Witness A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He resigned, Mr. Kordic, on the 25th of January --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm cutting stuff out, Your Honour, in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He resigned on the 25th of January from his position as deputy president. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The vice-president of HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the resignation was rejected at a meeting on the 27th. Do you know anything about that? This was the meeting where Kljuic was ousted and his authorities frozen, it appears.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we'll move on as swiftly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll give me a minute, I'll just try and cut material all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the man Skravan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Skravan. Did you know a man called Skravan Bozidar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please spell the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: S-k-r-a-v-a-n.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to March of 1992, and I want to come back briefly to Mr. Cicak. Mr. Cicak wrote newspaper articles, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know that he wrote things, but I don't know exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're here saying that this man was of unsound mind in some way. I may have missed it in the newspaper articles, but was he ever challenged at the time of behaving in the way he did and writing in the way he did, simply because of weakness of intellect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone can write whatever they want wherever they want. Nobody ever prevented him from doing so, because there is no point responding to everything that appears in the press. That at least is my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cicak, on, for example, I'll just take one date, the 21st of March of 1992, challenged the legality of what you had all done because there had been no referendum of the Croat people. Now, first of all, we know that he was right, there had been no referendum. You've confirmed that already; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no referendum. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, apologies. I am trying to avoid any objections, but here we're talking about March 1992, and the question of referendum refers to May of 1992, and that is not clarified through the questions. It creates confusion. Could the questions be asked in a more precise way, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Naumovski, but I think that the question was more general. I do not think that any date was mentioned. That was a question that touched upon -- that was touched upon -- ago whether there were elections or not in the government, and the answer was that the government was not elected in the elections. Now, Mr. Nice, will you please ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What Mr. Cicak was objecting to, and you must remember this, is that the parastate or whatever it was that you had created, was illegitimate, was without democratic foundation. That's what he was complaining about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Cicak is concerned, or anyone else for that matter, everybody has the right to say what is legal and what is not legal. If some institutions are unable to operate in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the people are forced to fight for their survival and is creating -- is building up a structure in order to prevent from being expelled from the territory, I don't see what you can prefix with para, because everybody was fighting for their survival in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and everybody has to express -- can express their view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Maric. Will you please try to confine yourself to answers to questions that are asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to deal with that last point, if Ms. Verhaag will hold up the three volumes of the lists for -- the government of Sarajevo was publishing laws for the years 1992, 1993, and 1994. Well published. It was still a functioning government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct that they are still enforced today. In 1992 and 1993 the laws could not reach my office in Busovaca, let alone other places. Those laws could reach only as far as the city of Zenica, which was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the record, they're called Sluzbeni lists. I must move at speed. This man, Cicak, and this is really susceptible to a yes/no answer, was challenging the legitimacy of what you had all done, and he was entirely entitled to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Croatian people, this was legitimate, because we fought for the interests of Croatian people in the territory which were ours and for which we -- and where we fought to also allow others to live, because we were at risk. Bosnia and Herzegovina was splitting up. The units of JNA had already taken 70 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you won't answer that question, answer this one. Why was Mr. Cicak beaten up, please, merely for the expression of democratic views?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the fact that he was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Really? As mayor, you had no knowledge of the fact that he had been beaten up, that he had complained to Kordic that he had a newspaper article published saying Kordic's men had done it? No awareness of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you on holiday in March of 1992, away from your territory or something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1992 I was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not telling this Chamber the truth, are you, because when the truth is impossible, you have to hide behind amnesia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth about what I know. That is my truth. You can judge for yourself whether this is the truth or not. I have given a solemn declaration and I'm speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you decline or are unable to help this Chamber at all with the detail of what happened to the man publishing articles in favour of democracy, but you nevertheless assert against him that he's a person of mental illness, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what my personal views are on Mr. Cicak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on the question of Mr. Cicak's mental illness, the witness had said earlier that he had formed the conclusion that Mr. Cicak was mentally ill because Mr. Cicak had told him that he couldn't fulfill some of his duties. I wanted to ask the witness whether there was anything else. Was there anything in the conduct of Mr. Cicak himself that led you to believe that he was mentally ill?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cicak showed me this certificate and told me that he had been ill, that he had a lot of problems. He had headaches and he had problems with his behaviour. And if somebody would oppose him, he would lose control very quickly. He would become angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When do you say he told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met in '89, we met, and in 1990, I said that he was a member of the Busovaca HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you're saying he told you all this before you voted him into office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If Mr. Cicak had not himself told you this, would you have formed the impression that he was mentally ill?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the person who volunteers this information to me. I can have my own view about the person, but when a person tells me the truth, then what he tells me I take to be the truth. And then he also was entering into arguments, and, for instance, if he reacted in a certain way, later on he would say, "I did not want to react in this certain way." He couldn't control himself. I knew this man well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This didn't stop you from voting with him, if the article in Slobodna Bosna of the 22nd of May of 1999 is right, it didn't stop you voting with him against Kordic's election, did it, at an early stage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What vote? I did not quite understand what vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were quoted in that newspaper article as having voted with Florijan Glavocevic and Mr. Cicak against Kordic's election as National Defence Secretary and HDZ General Secretary. Is the newspaper article right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must move forward, I'm afraid. Let's come to the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please see Exhibit Z76.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document by way of a receipt for weaponry. Do you remember the circumstances in which Mr. Kordic obtained these particular weapons? They're signed, you see, by his name, at the bottom of the receipt.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know that in the Lasva Valley there are two large factories; BMT produced weapons and Vitezit produced explosives, all kinds of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short because we've heard a lot about this. He demanded these very substantial weapons, didn't he, and he did it in April of 1992 and he wouldn't take no for an answer; do you know that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, that that is how it was framed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of how he was the person signing for this heavy weaponry when he was merely a politician, or just a politician?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the defence office in Busovaca in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I thought you carefully explained to us that the defence office has very limited military functions. Can you explain, please, why this politician was getting heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
