utterances.text: At that time Mr. Dario Kordic worked in the Busovaca municipality where he held the post of the Secretary of National Defence; that is the position he was holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the Draga barracks. The Draga barracks were emptied of their weapons by the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there was a distribution. I explained in my testimony that there are three barracks in the municipality Busovaca; that at Kacuni, that is, weapons and buildings were overtaken by Muslim units --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want you to repeat your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm not repeating my testimony. All I want to say is Draga was allotted to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the taking of weapons from the Draga, did the JNA do something unpleasant?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because it bombed Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you missed out is what happened in between. What happened to the soldiers from the JNA barracks, that is, the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present when they were evacuating Draga, and as soon as the soldiers had started on their way to Sarajevo on a bus, I took my car and drove home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this operation, you were in plain clothes but Kordic was by now wearing a uniform, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did wear a uniform, but anyone could put it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers, were they taken off somewhere else into the countryside, to a fate, at the time, unknown?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, the JNA soldiers, as you know, were not taken anywhere. They headed for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The commander of this operation was Kordic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the takeover of the Draga barracks, the crisis staff was in operation then and it was Mr. Florijan Glavocevic and Mr. Hadzimejlic who were designated to take care of the takeover from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The taking of these weapons from the JNA was by surprise; it was effectively by ambush, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not sudden because an agreement had been reached a long time before that. My part of the crisis staff, headed by me, we discussed it with JNA representatives at the Rajlovac barracks. And I can tell you that I was detained on that road by the former JNA, that is, by the forces of the SDS, on the Ilijas bridge, and I was to be liquidated then, me and Mr. Milorad Jovic, Mr. Glavocevic, and Mr. Hadzimejlic; that is, Asim Sunulahpasic and the commander of the then chief of police, Husnija Neslanovic, they can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that it was this early miscalculation of the approach to the Draga barracks that led to the JNA's response into the bombing of Busovaca, and that this was all probably led by Kordic; you don't accept that, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I repeat, sir, Your Honours, Kordic did not run that operation. The operation was run by Mr. Glavocevic and Mr. Hadzimejlic regarding the takeover of the weaponry and the barracks from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come to the next incident, which is the Kaonik camp weapons on May the 9th. The agreement was simply for an equal share of weapons, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was reached to share it 50/50, that is, half to go to the Croat and half to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The checkpoint that had been erected, before any armed conflict between you and the Muslims, was a solely HVO checkpoint, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was in the territory with the Croat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why wasn't it a joint checkpoint if you were still trying to cooperate with the Muslims at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the territories where the Croats were controlling had Croat majorities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you that all that happened was that the Muslims arrived all in one truck to collect the weapons. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came, as there had been an agreement on the takeover, the Muslims, that is, the majority who had not agreed, because they were headed by Mr. Dzemal Merdan at the Leptir, and I told you yesterday in detail how it all happened. So they wanted to force their entry into the Kaonik barracks so as, in point of fact, to take it over, notwithstanding the agreement, because it was said that 50 per cent of the weaponry should go to the Muslims and 50 per cent to the Croats. And they came to the Leptir disco to take it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that what you're saying about a breach of the agreement is made up by you and others in order to try and justify what happened then and thereafter, and they simply turned up to take the weapons they had agreed should be theirs.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm telling the truth, because I know, I was a participant in these matters, because I headed the crisis staff, and I know how the action was carried out to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, then, look at Z100, please, and hear your account on that and your view on it. Just to remind us, I think this is a document that you participated -- in the drafting of which you participated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But that you felt unwell before it was completed, and therefore you had to go home before it was signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with at which stage of the document's drafting you started to feel unwell, how much of it we can see as a reflection of your input and how much is after you had to go home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was drafted -- the whole document was drafted. I left before it was signed. But all it says here was agreed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And then let's come to the signatures, because I just want to be quite sure what you're saying about Mr. Kordic's signature. Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that Mr. Ivo Brnada, commander of the municipal HVO staff, military wing, signed this, and Mr. Dario Kordic was only a co-signatory to this. This is a document as a surety, as a guarantor, that it was verified --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to show that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where does the document say that, please? You're an educated man. We've all seen documents that say "signed in the presence of so-and-so" or "witness." Where does it say that Kordic is signing as -- I think it's a guarantor, is it? Co-signatory or guarantor: Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among us it is a practice, it is a practice with us, that the person who signs the act signs it on the right-hand side, and the person who is witness to that signs on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And so we'll have to have a look at a few more orders if that's really your evidence. But let's see what you think about the content of this document after these years and can help us with. Unilateral -- paragraph 1 -- the unilateral termination of the agreement decided that HVO should take all the weapons. Why was that, then? Just because the other side had shown, on your account, an inclination to take more weapons from Kaonik? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they did not comply with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the paramilitary formations, the so-called -- number 3: To be given an ultimatum to hand over all their weapons? Why was that imposed? You weren't yet at war with these people. Why were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were falling foul of the agreement. But I must point out that the TO never came under the HVO. And after these events between the 9th and 10th of May, they continued to exist in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well, I'm not going to have time to deal with that for the time being, but let's go on to number 4. No HVO representative has the right to negotiate with representatives of the so-called Territorial Defence and the Patriotic League. Why so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that agreement was not observed, and if you reach an agreement that something has to be done in such-and-such way, then how can one say there is -- how does one proceed to try to reach an agreement if what has been agreed is not observed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then of course the arrest of the three men. Do you remember telling His Honour Judge Robinson yesterday, I think it was, who would be carrying out the arrest? The police, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to whom did they respond? I think you told His Honour the civil side; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police was to arrest them, that is, to take them in for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you say that it is under Brnada or under --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you say that these police are under Brnada, under Kordic, or under you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police operated under the civilian HVO. As a matter of fact, the crisis staff was still active that evening. The civilian police were still under the supervision of the civilian wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So who is that, you or Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of the crisis staff. I told you that. And when this was signed, then the crisis staff practically ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document was another step on the way of a takeover of power by an unelected body, wasn't it? Quite simple.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "unelected" and "illegal," Your Honours, you should know that at such times when you have a crisis on your hands, then there can be no referendum, as you say. It takes time to have a referendum. And these are all pre-war conditions practically, because there was bombing, and there were all sorts of things which are difficult to describe now what the situation was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why was Merdan beaten up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he was beaten up. I know that he was interrogated, because he brought in fact people to Leptir illegally, who were not supposed to take part in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then this period of time started on the 11th of May, ended just what, 11 or 12 days later, didn't it, with Z111? If we can look at that, please, Z111.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kordic's signature on the left-hand side. This is in the witness position, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see that there's been a blockade of the city of Busovaca in all directions for the preceding 10 days, and that's now abolished. There's a curfew introduced. We'll come back to number 3 in a minute. Number 4, because the HVO of the Busovaca municipality is leading the whole -- I'm so sorry to the interpreters if I'm going too fast -- the whole organisation of life and defence. The Busovaca Municipal Crisis Command will not do their duties anymore, nor will they take any decisions. This was a takeover, wasn't it, by your party, through the HVO, of your region?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat Defence Council took over all competencies in order to assume all responsibility for developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, under item number 3, about the workers of government bodies and municipal assembly workers and of companies immediately organised functioning of the governmental bodies of the Busovaca Municipal Assembly. What about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will remember that there's got to be an amendment from the English version of the translation of the passage in brackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you interpret number 3 as doing, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for number 3 here, where it speaks about the desire to organise the life in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, and invites all workers, all employees, to work in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca without coercion, so that everybody can do their jobs as they wanted to do before. Because I'm telling you, the situation was very difficult and it was increasingly grave from one day to the other, and we were trying to organise it through these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had evidence in this Court of people saying they were only allowed to return to work, or would only have been allowed to return to work, on terms of an oath of loyalty to the HVO. What do you say to that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked anyone to sign loyalty. Everybody could come and work as he pleased, so nobody ever demanded that anybody sign any loyalty, whether he would be loyal or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you think of anything that was being said by officials or by the proprietors or directors of enterprises? Can you think of anything that was being said to Muslims that they could have misunderstood as a requirement to give an act of fidelity or an oath of fidelity to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as I'm aware, nobody ever requested that anybody sign any kind of fidelity to anyone. I've already said that. I say it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There weren't any particularly enthusiastic or committed local people who might have used the changed circumstances as a way of getting rid of Muslim employees, if they weren't prepared in some way to sign up to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Nobody ever, never, ever, asked anyone to sign any kind of loyalty. What was pursued was to have people work, to have some kind of peace in the municipality of Busovaca, because the situation was getting graver from one day to the other, and the Croats and Bosniaks and Serbs who lived in those territories had to see that this be organised to the benefit of every man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, the period of time between this change of circumstances and the end of the year is covered by the documents that you provided yesterday. I may have a few questions to ask you about those after the lunch adjournment, but I'm not in a position to do so at the moment. But tell us, between whatever we're up to now, May 1992 and the end of the year, were people leaving the territory? Muslims, were they leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also the displaced persons were arriving. I only have to tell you that my family, my wife and my children, were away because there was shelling. The situation was complicated: war in Croatian, war in the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so people feared for their life. Everybody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this intervening period, the second half of 1992, perhaps the witness could just help us by looking at a couple of exhibits. Exhibit 120, please. You're telling us, I think, that Mr. Kordic had no military function of any kind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that Mr. Kordic never had anything military. He was only a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to bother with more than one of these documents, but it's just to give the witness an opportunity to deal with one obvious point. If 120 hasn't yet been produced, can I produce it and I'll provide copies later? If I separate it out, original for the witness and English copy for the ELMO. Sorry. I hadn't appreciated it hadn't gone in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you're looking at there is an order of June 1992, so the same period of time, which says: "The municipal headquarters of the Defence Council in Vares is ordered to send a unit of 30 soldiers immediately on receipt of this order to protect the village of Tarcin Do because of an immediate danger of Chetniks attacking the village." And then it's said the units are obliged to stay in the village until weapons are secured. Now, that's a military instruction, isn't it? Do doubts about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's nevertheless a military instruction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be a political one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Ordering a unit of soldiers to move for purposes of defence of a village, is that the sort of thing that politicians were doing regularly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were instances of politicians, because they are concerned for their people, so they would organise higher alertness so that people can defend their lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I don't understand that. But let me -- my mistake, I'm sure. But help me with this: If this is a military order affecting whatever it is, a platoon of 30 soldiers, where is the military signature that gives authority to this instruction? It's not there, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that this is the first time I see this. I know that the gentleman was a politician, and perhaps there was a military component from the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you see the difficulty, don't you? This is signed by Kordic; it's signed on the right-hand side of the page, just in case there's any significance in the difference. This man was giving military instructions, wasn't he? Wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, and political too. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be good enough to look at this photograph. It doesn't come out terribly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I've got the copy immediately available for the ELMO, if that helps, 2703.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, it appears from the background, if you have a look at it closely, this may be up in the Tisovac area. At what part of the period 1992/1993 did you see Mr. Kordic dressed like this, looking like this, and carrying a weapon of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody could put on a military uniform, I told you; I also wore it for a time. You should know that at any moment, a man -- even if he was not wearing a uniform, because 14-year-old children to 60-year-old men defended the territories of the municipality. And if a man walks around in civilian clothes, he cannot be in civilian clothes, he had to wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not actually an answer to the question. What part of the period 1992/1993 did you see Mr. Kordic dressed like this and did you see him carrying a gun like this, this politician?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only had a photograph taken of him with the rifle, because he didn't carry one. I know that whenever he would come he never had any weapons. This was just posing for the picture. I also had a picture taken of me with a weapon in the former army, to have it as a memento.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, the question is simple so will you please try to avoid any comments. Did you see Mr. Kordic dressed like this, as a military man, and carrying a weapon, as this photograph shows? Did you ever see him like that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic did wear a military uniform but did not carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At what period of the history did he start being called "Colonel"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started addressing him like that when he first went to Sarajevo for discussions with the representatives of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the period of time at which he was falling out with Blaskic and starting to take over military authority from Blaskic, as I must suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Messrs. Kordic and Blaskic were never --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last word. It didn't come out audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat for the transcript what you just said, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, Messrs. Kordic and Blaskic never had a dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to that at the end. I'll pass over the balance of 1992 for the time being and come to 1993, and I'll return to 1992 this afternoon if time allows. You tell us in your summary, and I think in evidence, something about Dzemal Merdan instigating a crisis by complaining about a machine-gun. The truth is that in that period of time, 1992 and into 1993, the HVO did patrol with machine-guns on vehicles, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a truck with a machine-gun mounted on it which patrolled from one checkpoint to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It also patrolled in the areas of town, in particular in the Muslim areas.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. They went from the checkpoint at the Busovaca-Kiseljak municipal boundaries towards Zenica, to a place called Grablje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were also machine-guns, as we've heard from a witness called (redacted), that were posted in the Muslim areas. What about that; true or false?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, how, then, does Merdan's complaining about a machine-gun have any bearing on what we've been inquiring into?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Merdan had in mind when he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not what Mr. Merdan said -- I'm sorry, I must sort this out -- it's what you said. I may have misunderstood it. Paragraph 34. You said this in paragraph 34, you said, "At about the 15th of January of 1993, I went to Kacuni to speak with Dzemal Merdan who had instigated a crisis because an HVO truck with a machine-gun mounted on it was patrolling the road from Kaonik to Kacuni. Claiming that it irritated them, the Muslim troops stopped the truck." Well, was that a crisis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a crisis because Kacuni was already filled with the displaced persons who were getting ready for a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's your evidence that people were getting ready for a conflict as opposed to merely protecting themselves from an increasingly all-powerful local government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't take it any more. I showed you a number of documents yesterday where the government made efforts to achieve normalcy of life, and you could see that 30 tonnes of flour was distributed on a Friday before the conflict which broke out between Sunday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness see 381.4; coming your way. Your Honour, of course I'm not going to introduce more than the necessary minimum of documents, but I must give the witness, as I try generally, the opportunity to deal with contemporaneous accounts from independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document you almost certainly will not have seen before. It's a document from the army that was patrolling the area at the time. I'm afraid it is only in English, and I'll read out the relevant passage to you slowly enough for you to follow it, I trust. It's on the second page, at number 9, in a document that is dated itself the 20th of January, 6.00 in the evening. This document says: "The Dutch Transport Battalion report that tensions in Busovaca have increased recently. The BiH commander was stopped in the town by the district HVO police and his weapons and car were taken from him." Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was also reported: "The HVO police in Busovaca had been reinforced by HVO from elsewhere." Was that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was wondering whether there was any reason for reinforcing at exactly that time, in January of 1993. You say the Dutch Battalion's report or information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information is not correct. There were displaced people in Busovaca who had arrived from Jajce and other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I -- sorry. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no units there in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see 382.3; coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 21st of January but it is retrospective to a degree. It's a milinfosum, that is, a military report document, and it says these things about your town. On the first page, at number 2: "On the 18th of January, an ICRC convoy was stopped at Busovaca by an HVO checkpoint. The drivers were Muslims from Zenica. They were intimidated and robbed. As they subsequently drove away, shots were fired at them causing two tyres to be punctured." True or false?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that event. I was the civilian part of the HVO and the checkpoint was manned by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you should say what ICRC is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: International Committee of the Red Cross. You understood that, did you? I'm sorry if you didn't. The ICRC was a Red Cross convoy.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had said that I did not know about that event because the checkpoints were manned by military policemen. So I cannot speak to that event because I don't know about it. Because I was the civilian HVO, I did not receive that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, number 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, sorry to interrupt you. Mr. Maric, are you telling us that there was absolutely nothing in common between the civilian wing of the HVO and the military wing of the HVO, that there was no mutual information/feedback between the two?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the structures were established, the military was brought into a military chain of command and the civilian was separated out. So everybody was accountable for their own sector; the military to the military structure and the civilian police to the civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I'm not interested in the chain of command. I'm talking merely about information. Wasn't there information which circulated from one wing to the other wing of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the stopping in your small town of a Red Cross convoy, with the intimidation and robbing of Muslim drivers, was something that could happen without even coming to your attention; is that really what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any intimidation, any, as you put it -- I don't know how you put it -- I condemn such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second page, item 6, this is what the International Observers, Mr. Maric, said about the Kacuni checkpoint. They said that "The BiH in Busovaca have established a checkpoint at Kacuni. This is the only BiH checkpoint between Vitez and Kiseljak and is located just north of the BiH Brigade headquarters. It is manned by 15 to 20 soldiers with automatic weapons and an RPG-7. Anti-tank mines are also said to be laid at the checkpoint." Now, is that about accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They had a checkpoint at Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the description of the number of soldiers and equipment is about right, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that occasionally there were even more; 20, and up to 30 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever go there yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I spoke to Mr. Dzemal Merdan, before the conflict, and I also -- based on the information I received, even the UNPROFOR representatives mentioned this checkpoint, because at that time I had contacts with them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to the 20th of January of 1993, and I think you volunteered or were asked about and told us something about an incident occurring at a checkpoint involving another politician; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I received, Mr. Ignac Kostroman had been stopped at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date? The date of the incident, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th or 21st. I don't know exactly but I think it was more likely the 20th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help me, please, with this: You're not the first witness whose chosen a base of dates, a bracket of dates, of the 20th/21st. What is it that fixes one of two dates in your mind, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not why I choose it. This is what was happening. The crisis was intensifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why, when asked about something, do you say, "Well, it was either the 20th or the 21st"? For example, have you discussed this with the other witnesses in the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that -- the information came and I -- and this was seven years ago. I cannot recall exactly, but I know that the shelling started on the 25th, when the fiercest fighting took place in Busovaca. And at the same checkpoint the day before, on the 24th, Mr. Ivica Petrovic was killed, and another gentleman, a taxi driver, also was killed at that checkpoint on the 24th. And early on the 25th, and I mentioned that yesterday, there was heavy attack of the Bosniaks on Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what do you say you were told had happened to this politician on the 20th or 21st?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he had been stopped and harassed, that he was prevented from reaching his destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discover how it was that the incident ended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have detailed information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That same night did anything else happen that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Muslim premises were blown up and that Mr. Mirsad Delija was seriously injured and that unfortunately he died on route to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, those attacks, both on the shop premises and on Mirsad Delija, they were connected to the incident at the checkpoint, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the result of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake for not following the answer. The attacks on the shop premises and the attack on Mirsad Delija followed from the incident at the checkpoint, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because they were by way of reaction to interference with a politician at the checkpoint. That's what you mean, isn't it? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ignac Kostroman was harassed at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that led -- I'll come back to that in a minute, but on your evidence, that led to the destruction of the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It resulted in -- this incident resulted in people who were in that area. It angered them, so they went and they blew up these premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then they went and murdered Delija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't murdered; he was seriously injured. He died on the way to hospital. That is the report that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was called out of his house and shot and he died. Isn't that murder?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a murder, since the man eventually died. I condemn such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But for the avoidance of any doubt -- we've now got to it -- these acts on the people of Busovaca, their premises, and the man Delija, flowed from the incident at the checkpoint incident involving a politician?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of who it was, yes, it was a politician who was there. But I condemn any kind of excessive acts. I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Delija died because it was his brother who had stopped the politician, and the murderers went to his family home and they found the wrong brother. That's about right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get such a report. What I can say is what I see for myself and what is presented to me, and this was presented to me in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the fact that this attack on Busovaca Muslims was connected to the stopping of a politician was well-known, was common currency, in the conversation of Busovaca at the time; correct? We've already heard other evidence about there being rumours about this, but please confirm it. It was well-known, it was talked about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told me what you discovered through being in, of course, a position of some authority and having an inquiry and so on, but I still want an answer to the question, please. The fact that these attacks were retaliation for what had happened to a politician were well-known and widely discussed in Busovaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I mentioned what the report on that incident was that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you won't answer that question, will you answer this one: But the rumours at the time were that the politician was not Kostroman, but Kordic who was stopped; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Kostroman who was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, then, about this report: You received a report. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That report is in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same archive as that from which these documents come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the entire archive is at the municipality, and I left the municipality in 1994, in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And have remained an active politician, in various guises, in the same area ever since?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I remained an active politician and continue to be so, and I am a representative in a legislative body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might that be a convenient moment? And although I shall have to excise a considerable number of topics, I think, in the circumstances, I can properly do so and conclude by the end of the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice, for being so cooperative and for the way in which you conducted your cross-examination. Of course, you are always entitled to ask all the relevant questions. That you do. We appreciate the way you did it. And now we shall adjourn. We shall make a break and we shall resume at half past 2.00. We shall work until half past 4.00. I am not -- now, I am not encouraging you, but if you will need additional time, then Judge Robinson and I shall be ready to consider it. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that Judge Robinson drew my attention to a problem of translation from French into English. I said, "Thank you, Mr. Nice, for being so cooperative," but I did not say in French "for the way you conducted your cross-examination." It was the interpreter who added that. So would you please strike that out, what I said, "Thank you for your cooperation," and what I meant was by taking care of the time. I also wanted to thank you, Mr. Nice, for condensing your cross-examination within the time frame. I also said that it wasn't a matter of five or ten minutes; you can always, if necessary, use a couple of minutes more in order to enable this witness to be able to leave this weekend from The Hague. So that was what I wanted to say. Mr. Nice, please go on now with the cross-examination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Response obscured by translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 381.3, please, coming up. This is a document, the very last page of which is almost illegible in the copy form produced. I have the original here. It's barely more legible there but I've been able, or to be precise, Ms. Verhaag has been able to make out most of what's there, and I'll read it out what it contains for completeness. Mr. Maric, this is a military document, the 20th of January of 1993, and it deals with Busovaca on the third page, at the foot of the third page, and it reads as follows: "The BiH in Busovaca area have erected a new checkpoint at Kacuni. This is the only checkpoint on route from Vitez to Kiseljak and is located north of the brigade headquarters, manned by approximately 15 to 20 soldiers who are equipped with automatic weapons." That's what we heard, I think, before. It goes on to say that: "Reports from the soldiers during daylight hours stated that the BiH had laid" -- now the last page is illegible on the copy form, but it reads roughly like this -- "a number of mines at the checkpoint," and then there's reference to information from the Dutch that the mines had been lifted as darkness fell, and the comment that "this is another indication of the spread of mistrust through the Busovaca-Travnik-Vitez area." Would you agree with those comments of the military men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the comment these are units which were coming there and they could see, if it says so, about what happened at the checkpoint, that is proof to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 385, which is already an exhibit, and this, Mr. Maric, is a document dated the 21st of January, but it's retrospective to a limited degree. It says of Busovaca, on page 2, the following, and I'll read it slowly. It refers to the earlier document, and it then says: [as read] "Dutch report that the new BiH checkpoint in Kacuni was put in place to prevent HVO reinforcements coming from Kiseljak or Kresevo. The local BiH commander states that these reinforcements arrived during the evening of the 20th of January and were turned back at the checkpoint." Now, is that correct? This is a contemporaneous document and a contemporaneous complaint by the BiH. Is that why the checkpoint was put up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I hear about these documents. I know that no units, apart from those that were in Busovaca, ever arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but is it right that reinforcements were coming from Kiseljak and Kresevo and that was what concerned the BiH commander? You were there. Please help us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it because I was not aware of that, and there were no reinforcements coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It goes on to say this: "Tensions increased in Busovaca during late afternoon. Between 2000 and 2100 hours, two HVO checkpoints were erected at either end of the town centre. At approximately the same time a quad 4 by .5, mounted on a flatbed," and that, I think, is a shorthand description of a weapon mounted on a flatbed lorry, "was deployed on the road south of the town. All main routes in and out of Busovaca were then controlled. Between 2100 and 2.00 the following morning," I summarise, "the Dutch reported a number of explosions, and on the 21st, the daylight recce," reconnoitre, "confirmed that eight shops or kiosks had been badly damaged by fire and some form of explosives. The Dutch believe that these shops, which are all Muslim, were possibly damaged by grenades. Both HVO checkpoints were removed on the 21st of January. A local source reported to the Dutch Battalion that a number of families in Busovaca had sent their children to stay with friends in Zenica," and the comment was, "the action of the 20/21 of January appears to be a preplanned, coordinated attack on the Muslim population." Now, are there any facts in what I have read out to you that you dispute?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that date, it is not true at all that there was any shelling. Yes, there was tension, and I've already pointed out that that evening some shops were blown up by explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you don't challenge, as the man on the spot at the time, disagree with anything that's said in that report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with all of it. Something is correct in part because, yes, there were shops which blew up. Not only Muslim; there were also Croat shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Next Exhibit, please, is 392. And while they're coming to you, Mr. Maric, I'm presenting to you the contemporaneous views of independent observers so we can, through you, get a correct account of what was happening on these important days. This document is dated the 25th of January, and it's another military document, but it reviews matters that have happened in the previous seven days. And on the third page it simply says again, at letter F: "Tension between Muslims and Croats increased at the beginning of the week. On the 20th of January, 1993, a new roadblock was established by the Bosnian army near Kacuni, manned by 20 soldiers with automatic weapons, in order to reduce the level of HVO reinforcements from Kiseljak/Kresevo." So again it's the same point. Perhaps I needn't actually have troubled with that one. My error. Now, what you tell us is, amongst other things, and this is paragraph 37 of your affidavit, you say there was an attack on the 25th of January, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, 1993, the attack of Muslim forces on Busovaca began in the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you were, and the other officials in Busovaca, in contact from time to time with the military people who drove by in their white vehicles, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also tell us, unless -- I think, in relation to this part of the history, that there were lists obtained from a captured Muslim soldier containing the names of neighbours who were to be liquidated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see this document yourself or is this the stuff of rumour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not rumours. I saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is the document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be at the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Such a document, if it is existed, is exactly the sort of document that you would show to the military -- the independent international military observers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said when the conflict broke out, that is, on the 25th, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Podjele. I spent there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question again. The type of document you describe having seen is exactly the sort of document that the warring parties, if and when they became warring parties, would show to UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I wanted to explain. It was some 15 days later that I met the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you see the document? Who had it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the military police at the time was Mr. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So Mr. Cosic was in a position to give an account of this and to show the document to the UNPROFOR if he had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he communicated with UNPROFOR, but I did see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He could either communicate with UNPROFOR or he could communicate with the military in Busovaca, couldn't he? This is an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was the civilian authority in Busovaca, so that as far as military matters are concerned, it's up to military units. It's within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you saw this list. What did it say? Did it have a title on the top: "Neighbours to be liquidated"? Or how do you know what it was? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document said that every neighbour should shoot his neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An absolutely astonishing document; you'll agree with that, won't you? An extraordinary thing to see, even in the troubled times of Busovaca and Central Bosnia; yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that is, to kill a man, a man to kill a man, and they lived together until a few moments ago, that's a disgrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by whom was this document signed, or where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who signed it. The order was not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in any event -- it wasn't signed? What did you say? You first of all said, "I don't know who signed it," and then you said, "The order wasn't signed." Well, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who signed it, because it is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the document should still exist in someone's archive. Whose archive is that? The police archive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And where may that archive be found, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know exactly. I'm telling you that in 1994 I left Busovaca from those parts, so that I can't know where it is. The archive should be in Busovaca, but where is it now? I do not know how you came by the documents that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And being shown this document, you weren't shown it on the basis that you shouldn't tell anyone else about it. Presumably, once you saw it, you had to tell other people; it was such an astonishing document. Wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who should I tell about it when I didn't communicate at the time? I'm telling you that it was about 15 days later that I spoke to the leaders of the SFOR, or rather the then UNPROFOR. And I didn't have the document with me to say, "Here, look what's being done."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And since you see the point that's coming, at no time have you ever mentioned the existence of such an astonishing document to the International Community, with whom you regularly spoke; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what I see and show, so that I can document it to every person. But at that time I did not have the document with me to present it to the gentlemen that I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 395.2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 395.2, please, with my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, there was no attack by the BiH. As we're going to see from the independent observers, there turned out to be exchanges, but there was no attack. This is a document dated the 25th of January -- yes, 25th, 26th -- and at item 17 on page 4 of the document, as we have it, it says this about Busovaca: "The situation in Busovaca deteriorated. Several roads in the area were declared out-of-bounds for humanitarian convoys by UNPROFOR. A BiH army roadblock at Gusti Grab, near Busovaca, prevented all road movement north from Kiseljak. HVO and BiH forces around this village exchanged mortar and small arms fire, while some house burning began. HVO reportedly hold the high ground around and seem to be adopting a more aggressive attitude than the BiH forces." Do you have any quarrel with any of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 25th of January, 1993, in the morning, when it started, this fighting, I was at home. And you are telling me there was no shelling. I affirm there was, because dozens of shells fell on my village too. Snipers who were north of my house, that is, Strane, which is a Muslim area, snipers fired in the direction of my village. It was a fierce attack. And nobody can tell me that there was no shelling when I went through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, please, 423, coming your way. A slightly longer entry but it comes to the end of this period of time. On the first page of this document, which is dated the 30th of January, it sets out something about the arrangements made for a ceasefire in the Kacuni/Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I didn't really want to cut in. But in the middle paragraph which refers to meetings between the BiH and HVO, an annex A is mentioned, so that my objection is to the completeness of the document, because this document should also be accompanied by the annex if this document is to be used. It's the second passage, second paragraph, on the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, could you please help us? Could you please assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we have the annex, we'll produce it. I'm not sure if we've got it. I'm not certain we have. No. The document is all that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: What paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Foot of the first page, not the middle of -- I'm only covering the middle of the page for introductory purposes. I'm going to the third paragraph, paragraph 3, which sets out the findings in relation to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This reports in relation to Busovaca and Kacuni: "An LO team spoke with Edin Beganovic at the BiH headquarters of the 333rd Brigade at Kacuni. Edin stated he was the officer responsible for morale, information, and religion. He believed that the Muslims in Busovaca (between the ages of 16 and 65) had been arrested and detained either at the secondary school at Busovaca or the Mediapan factory. Edin reported the conflict had started when the Muslims had ignored the HVO demands to hand in their weapons on the 20th of January." I'm going to pause there for a minute. He's right in reporting, isn't he, that Muslims were required to hand in their weapons on the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware at all that anybody asked for weapons from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. It goes on, then, to say this: "Approximately 50 HVO extremists led by Anto Sliskovic were then reported to have destroyed many Muslim properties and to have killed one BiH soldier on the night of the 20/21 of January." Is it right that it was Sliskovic's men who committed the crimes you've told us about this morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose men were they.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You really can't help us at all.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot help you at all with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Edin reported that 50-100 BiH soldiers who lived in the northern part of Busovaca started to prepare defensive positions on Kardic hill. The HVO persuaded the BiH soldiers to give up their defensive positions and these soldiers were subsequently arrested." Can you confirm that is true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there were talks about a ceasefire, when that was supposed to be arranged, then it was said that all trenches should be covered, filled in; however, the Muslim units did not respect that, they went on digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So broadly speaking you accept the accuracy of this but you put a different interpretation on it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking the truth, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report of the International Observers goes on: "Edin stated that the 333rd Brigade's area of responsibility was the front line around Maglaj. Since tensions between Muslims and Croats had risen, these forces were withdrawn back to the Kacuni area. He stated they were keen to negotiate with the Croats in order to effect both body and prisoner exchanges." True?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the gentleman who is saying that. If it is true, why were they withdrawing towards Busovaca? Why weren't they defending the areas around Maglaj, from whence they came? In other words, they were supposed to attack the Croats; that is what one can conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's read on and see what the other side said. "The liaison officer team returned to Busovaca and spoke to the HVO commander Jadsinovic. He stated that Lendo's forces, that is to say, the forces of the BiH from Novi Travnik, had attacked the Croat village of Busovaca from the direction of," and then he gives a direction, "at 1500 hours today," and the day of the report is the 30th of January, "resulting in three Croat deaths." Now, is that part of it true or false?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "He claimed to have intercepted a fax message from Lendo to Mekic which listed the five positions in Busovaca which should be attacked. He stated that BiH artillery positions in the village of Grablje shelled Busovaca." Now, is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That report says that the BiH troops were attacking. We only defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was reading it out for you for comment if there's anything wrong, you see. It then goes on, if I haven't missed anything, "The shelling was at 1700 hours this evening resulting in one house being destroyed and two Croat deaths. Jadsinovic believed that the BiH had both 105- and 122-military artillery pieces, as well as 82- and 122-millimetre mortars. He stated that the front line between the HVO or BiH forces passed through," and then he sets out the villages concerned which I needn't trouble you with, unless anybody wants to know, at the moment. Now, does that appear to be accurate so far as what's being said on your side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We do not find there, in the narrative of these five days, a starting point for what happened other than the incident on the 20th of January with the blowing up of the premises and the murder of Delija. Now, was that what started all this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago how things developed, what the situation was in the Busovaca area, and I don't want to repeat myself. Whatever I said previously is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was one more that I want your comment on. Document 390.3, it's just slightly back a few days. My mistake. It's for the 25th of January. So again this is right in the middle of the time when you say there was an attack, and if we look at the first page and the first paragraph, about six lines down, where it's dealing with Bosnia, and Central Bosnia generally, but it says: "The Busovaca-Kiseljak route is now reported as clear for UN vehicles; however, the recommendation is that soft-skinned vehicles do not use this route either. BritBat will patrol the routes and try to establish when free passage for all vehicles is possible. The main problem on the Busovaca-Kiseljak route is in the village of Kacuni. This roadblock is controlled by the BiH," and then it deals with what the soldiers are going to do. At the third page, item 7, it says this, under the assessment of the command: "Busovaca area. Busovaca and the surrounding area has been the scene of fighting during the day between Croat and Muslim forces. The CO," commander officer, "has reported that he has seen 20 Muslim houses burning in the area. He assesses that this action represents ethnic cleansing by the Croats against the Muslims." True?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas mentioned up at Kacuni, where Croats lived, about 1.200 people were expelled there, I also mentioned that, and how many houses were burned. I also said in my outline how many Muslim houses were burned or damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are not figures that I'm in a position to, and I don't, accept. Let's move forward in time from January, reminding ourselves that it was in the beginning of March that you called on President Tudjman. Did you get any minutes of the meeting that you had with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anybody?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who has the minutes but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 in your summary deals with the imam. You gave us an account of how you had to take some time to think about whether he could go or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because I wanted the imam to be present in Busovaca because he was needed there. He was a religious leader, and whenever a religious leader leaves an area, those who follow him feel differently too without the hodza or imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discuss his predicament with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought for a long time what to do, because I know how someone can feel in a community where he is a minority. And then I reached a decision that Mr. Enver Prolaz could leave the area of Busovaca, and I regret his having left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was effectively a hostage for a time, as he was described by some of the international observers. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that he couldn't move, but, you know, these were wartime circumstances. Because everybody is concerned about their own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the reason you took some time was so that you could discuss it with Kordic, whose approval you required?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn now to April and to Ahmici. But before we come to Ahmici itself, I want you, please, to help us with what you say -- let me just find it -- about preparations made by the BiH before the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry about this. Will you just give me one second. A document has been incorrectly numbered, but I can press on while we're finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say was the development of -- what do you say was the chronology of events relating to Kuber and its significance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I provided information on how, in the afternoon hours, heavy attack was launched by the Muslim forces on Kuber, and Kuber is a feature which is exposed from the direction of Zenica, from where the ABiH units attacked the territory of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When do you say they went there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was in the afternoon hours of the 15th of April, 1993. Muslim forces from the direction of Zenica attacked the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were already, were they, on the 15th of April, on the feature mounting an attack? That's your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were already attacking, and then there was one area towards Vitez, that was one direction, and then from Kuber towards Podjele, and the areas adjacent to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They held this feature and were able to attack your hometown from it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They attacked the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you just told these Judges is quite untrue. Would you like to have a look, please, at Exhibit 684. It's an outstanding exhibit. While it's being found, let me make it quite clear, Mr. Maric. I'm suggesting to you that you've corrupted the order of events in order to try to give an excuse for what happened on the 16th of April at Ahmici and elsewhere, and that what you're saying is not true. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling the truth, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, of which you must have the original before you, is signed by Colonel Blaskic on the 16th of April, but not only on the 16th of April; late in the evening -- well, in the evening of the 16th of April, at 1945 hours. And it reads: "Battle orders for the defence of Kuber. Extremist Muslim forces are advancing from the direction of Gornje Zenica towards Kuber with the intention of taking Kuber or cutting it off. Your mission is to deploy reinforcements in Kuber with your best-prepared and ablest forces, and defend Kuber unflaggingly. Minimum force strength is a company. Coordinate your operations with the Viteska Brigade, because Kuber must not fall. Upon occupying the defence lines, report to me in writing." It speaks only of Muslim forces advancing and of a mission to take the feature.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the conflict started in the afternoon hours of 15th of April. That is when Kuber was attacked. That is when the fighting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you like to explain this document to us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is true. And on the 16th the ABiH army units were attacking Busovaca, and they were grouping and attacking every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What preparations for events on the 16th of April had been made by the military, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was the head of the civilian HVO. I have practically nothing to do with the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that the document I'd like to lay on the ELMO is untranslated because it is only just available. Perhaps not only just available. No, it's only just selected. But may I nevertheless lay one document on the ELMO. Mr. Naumovski wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just what we have been saying in principle, not to use the documents which have not been translated. I think that that is how our own documents were handled. So the objection is not to use the document because it does not have a translation attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nice. It is exactly what we had decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, unlike the position of the Defence, we can't know in advance what a witness is going to say; we can't then know everything that's going to be relevant. They're always in a different position, having had the statement for months or years. If a witness comes along and says he's never taken any part in military matters, and a document, a short document, exists which could show the contrary, in our submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's a document that we are just using, we decided also to put it on the ELMO and then let the witness read the document and we will use the interpretation, in case it is a short document, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might we have it for the witness to look at it while it's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a document about the Home Guard, it's signed by you, and there's one other to a similar effect where you, I think, are appointing people to the Home Guard. If you'd just like to look at this one as well on the ELMO. They needn't be produced. These are military matters and you're signing orders, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed this document because this was security of the facilities of vital interest, like the PTT, and the Home Guard units were supposed to protect it, to provide security for it, the Home Guards consisting of older men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I needn't bother with the other one, because I must make more speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that document was simply over the one signature, namely, your signature, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, my signature, because I wanted to protect the buildings of vital interest to the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 861, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask for a five-minute break. I am a diabetic and I need to use the bathroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which case we are going to make a break and we will be back at 3.40. So we'll start again at 3.40. --- Break taken at 3.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, I hope you're feeling better now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Needless to say, if you are not feeling well, if you have any problem during your testimony, please let us know. Mr. Nice, evidently we have to include the break and we shall work, therefore, until quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell the Court that to finish at a quarter past four will inevitably involve my simply pruning large chunks, and I won't be able to raise all issues I probably should. I'm in the Court's hands. But let me press on, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 861 is a certificate, if you'd like to look at it, please. Have you got the original in front of you? It's a certificate. I don't think he has got the original. It's only the English version on the ELMO. This is a certificate signed by you -- he should have 861.1 -- here it is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got it? That's the original, if you would just like to have a look at that, which is a document signed by you saying that HVO members should not harass a particular person who is a Muslim person, of course, and Grubesic, you, and Kordic signed the document. Harassment was going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the displaced persons from other areas kept arriving -- and I pointed out that first it was the displaced people from Jajce after the fall of Jajce, and then the Zenica Croats who were coming to the Busovaca municipality -- their numbers grew. They wanted to find shelter for themselves and they harassed the Bosniak/Muslim population, which we wanted to prevent at any cost, so as to prevent their being expelled from their homes and harassed in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says here, "Busovaca HVO members," not incomers. It couldn't be clearer. The HVO was harassing people in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, members of the HVO were people, Croats, who were coming -- who had found themselves there. They were incorporated into the Croatian armed forces. They came from Jajce, Zenica, and later on, Travnik. All this complicated the situation. They were incorporated into the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 926, please. While that's being found, I can tell you what it's about. It's about a meeting an independent observer had with the imam of Busovaca, and the imam spoke of you and he spoke of the problems of the Muslims in Busovaca. It's annex K in the witness McLeod's report. He spoke of asking you to give them, the Muslims, protection and to give them a telephone line, and complained of Muslims' houses being taken over by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would give that to Ms. Verhaag, she can find it, or it's annex K, whichever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was what the imam told the investigating person correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as what the imam said, I pointed out that the situation in Busovaca was difficult, that the displaced people who were seeking shelter for themselves were harassing the Muslim population. We did all we could to protect those displaced people and the local Muslim population because we did not want them to leave Busovaca, but unfortunately what happened was that they found themselves forced to leave. I asked the people who were evicting Muslims from the houses, I asked them why, and they said, "Well, where should I live? I was also expelled." It is terrible when --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat that. The imam also said that between the 20th and 23rd of April, five women of Ocenici, five women were killed and their houses were burnt; just yes or no. True?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you accept that the HVO were killing some people in the area in the time that we are discussing, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only the HVO who killed but the Muslim units at Kacuni were also killing. From Kacuni, dead bodies were arriving through Kacuni from the area controlled by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, a simple yes/no answer to my question would help us. In the period of time with which we are concerned, there were wholly unjustified killings of Muslims in your area by members of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, and I condemned such excesses. I condemn every killing regardless of who has committed it. Unfortunately that was the situation. People lost their loved ones, and his vengefulness and the evil side is awakened, and only those who experienced it can understand it. There were people who had lost three brothers. It is sad to look at all that. Everyone suffered regardless of who they were, a Croat or Bosniak. It was very sad. I hope it never repeats itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to show you one more document, I think, at the moment, and then I may turn -- well, one more document in the series. While we're dealing with what you're saying about crime, crimes were largely committed by conscripts, weren't they? They weren't committed by refugees.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said these conscripts were displaced people who arrived from those areas and who were looking for shelter for themselves. Had they not come, the situation in Busovaca -- speaking specifically about Busovaca -- had the displaced persons not arrived from the eastern Bosnia area, from the north, they all arrived and they were looking for shelter in a very confined area --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to have to stop you. We don't have that much time.
