In September of 1993, do you accept that you prepared a report on crime for the year, and at that stage, September, it was two murders, one rape, ten aggravated robberies, and six armed robberies, with ten cases of planting explosive devices, and that was the total that you recorded in a report you signed off, or somebody else's report but you signed it. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I have time I'll show it to you. Does it sound about right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I signed something if I don't look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that if I have time later. 1217.1, please. This is a document of the 27th of September. It's from the European Monitors; it relates to a meeting with you and how you were asked about the situation of the Muslims in the town. You said that they had difficulties to control the criminal elements between the refugees, about 7.500. You were trying everything to protect the remaining Muslims, of which you said there were about 100. You promised that an investigation would be done to find responsibility for the mosque. When asked if you'd met the imam to discuss the situation of the Muslims, you denied that and said you would probably do this after the investigation. And then there was this comment: "It seems that the imam is considered more as a hostage than as a conversation partner." Is that all accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, because I respect the imam as a man and I wanted him to stay in Busovaca, and I continue to respect him to date. I also wanted to conduct an investigation in order to uncover the perpetrators of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're reported as going on to say this. Asked your opinion considering a possible peace, you said: "As long as Mr. Izetbegovic wants more territory, there would be no agreement and the Croats in Central Bosnia would fight until the death, and the only Muslim leader who could reach an agreement would be Mr. Abdic, but they were aware that he hadn't enough power to influence the Muslim hardliners." Is that a correct reflection of your then views?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I said so, because Mr. Izetbegovic advocated a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina, and not taking into account Croats. And when Croats pointed out that there would be an exodus out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They then went to see the imam, and he said there were only 38 Muslims left in September. He was very afraid, and was even afraid of having had contact with the international observers. That's about right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably right, if he went to imam after our conversation, but I don't know, because I did not control him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In another of the International Community's reports, that I haven't got time to find and show you at the moment, you're recorded as referring to the fact that Muslims had a higher birth rate than Croats. Was that something that preyed on your mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the birth rate of Muslims is higher than Croats, but it doesn't mean anything taken out of the context. But there are facts whose birth rate is higher than whose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... International Community, did you, as is recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say, and I mentioned it. I don't know what the conversation was, but there is no dispute that the birth rate of Muslims is higher than that of Croats. I don't see anything bad in that. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You will be aware that in very recent weeks, documents have been being produced in Zagreb following the change in the government. Are you aware of that? It's in the newspapers extensively.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. What I follow in the media is what you said, but I did not see any publicly released document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time with which we are concerned, in 1993 and 1994, you were the president of the Busovaca HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the civilian side of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in any event, personalities like Kraljevic would be known to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Person Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic, I met him in mid-1993, I believe in mid-June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a document I'd like this witness' comments on, if it can be produced, please. I know that the Defence have either been provided with it directly from Zagreb or, alternatively, they've had it provided to them by a co-defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this unauthenticated document on the grounds of hearsay, double hearsay. It's not signed by anybody, we have no idea who prepared it, there's no indication of who prepared it, or when, and it's absolutely prejudicial. In the absence of a better foundation being laid for this document, we think that introduction of this document amounts to deprivation of the rights of the accused to confront his accuser. It's a violation of Article 21 and it's also a violation of Rule 89 (c) and (d). It has no probative effect, and the prejudicial effect is self-evident, from an anonymous source. So we object to it in the absence of the Prosecution laying a foundation as to who wrote it, and when, and proving it was based on firsthand knowledge rather than multiple layers of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the Court knows, the providers or potential providers of documents have not provided documents, have been obstructive and non-cooperative until very recently. If documents come into our hands late, it is no fault of ours. The fault can be traced elsewhere. These documents will, or may, feature in another way at a later stage in the case, of course. But where there's a witness who can plainly deal with the content of the report, the witness should have a chance to do so now rather than to have no opportunity, and for the document, if it goes in due course in another way, to go in without the advantage of his comments. The Court being professional Judges, as it from time to time reminds us, is able to deal with evidence on a contingent basis, but what is important is that this witness should be given the opportunity to deal with this document, and in particular with the passages that he should be expected to be knowledgeable about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are they coming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from Zagreb. In case there's any -- it may be that Your Honours haven't been following matters as revealed in the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, could you tell us, and will you please speak slower so we will be able to follow. And you tried to say several times: Are you challenging the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. We have absolutely no idea who prepared it, when it was prepared, what the sources of information were upon which it was prepared. It's not signed. We think it's a complete fabrication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, can you help us with the problem of authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment we are in a position to draw to your attention the stamp on the front of the page beside the reference to HIS and a signature, which is the Croatian Intelligence Service. We were able to tell you that this document has been provided to us, as indeed I know to Mr. Kovacic, from one of the providers -- the provider in Zagreb of documents at the moment. We would respectfully remind the Chamber that there is material going to show that the Defence lawyers have had access to sources in Croatia, as well as in the Federation, far longer than we have, and that prima facie this must be a genuine document. It's provided, as the Chamber will also recall, or may recall, either wholly or in part, pursuant to orders made by this Court for production of documents. Some of that's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, but very briefly. The Defence received this document only after it learnt from the press that it had been disclosed to the Prosecution and some other addresses. So we received this document after the Prosecutor's office. That is the first thing. Secondly, this document is copied, so that it seems both these pages belong to one and the same document. However, the original has this first page, and it looks indeed as it looks here. And the second page, which seems to be annexed, is this unsigned document, which doesn't show the source, which doesn't show who did what, and so on and so forth. And that is why we challenge the authenticity of the document which is annexed. So we are objecting to the annex because that is a document which has not been authenticated or anything. And the Defence, of course, is fully -- has all the grounds, all the reason, to believe that it was a fabricated document. We do not know, of course, the purpose behind it. So we had absolutely no advantage over the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear, and I believe that the Prosecution does have a document which I transmitted to them this morning, so probably it was not seen. There are two Defenses. We received the document from the government of Croatia, indeed from the office of the president, on May 20, and that was at least four weeks after the Prosecution got it. And that was after we entered a very bitter discussion with the government based on the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Listen. Listen, Mr. Kovacic. Wait. We are not going to start this discussion now, because it is already 10 past 4.00 and it is Friday also. Tell us, please: Do you have the same document -- this same document, and was it given to you by the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is one of five documents in a set which the government gave us on the 20th of May. Not the government. Let me be precise. The presidency, the office of the president of the state. There were five documents in one and the same sets. This is only one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have the same documents which were given you by the office of the president of the Republic of Croatia; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To be quite precise, Your Honour, I sent a letter, I guess, two days ago to the Prosecution where I asked the same fact, because I never saw -- I did not have -- I was not in the position to see what actually Prosecution got from the office of the president and what I got. I only presumed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But do you have this document which we're now examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was one of the set of five documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wanted to have something clarified. In the English copy, the person who signs on the first page -- there's no signature there, because it's the English copy, but when we look at the Croatian, you can see a signature. Is that person purporting to be the author of what follows on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. As we understand it, this is a report being provided by the director of HIS to Tudjman, but the report itself is not signed off by that individual. So it is an enclosure or an attachment. It's a separate document. So -- at least that's my understanding of the position. So the document is a document as a whole and is to be construed in that way. But does he specifically sign off the report? No, he doesn't, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: So we don't know who is the author of the document here attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. We don't know who is the author, whether it's the same or a different person, but it is sent under the authority of the person signing and emerges from the archives of the state in the way that I've described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What indicates that it is sent under the authority of the person signing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because of how -- well, because it goes with it, because it's forwarded with it. The two documents are associated together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Did you receive it from the presidency of Croatia as it is now, as you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. We received it as the two pieces of paper, first that side and then separately that sheet. They're not one sheet of paper; they're two separate sheets of paper, again, as I understand it, but they're associated together as covering document and report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, we shall admit this document but in the fashion that you were given it, that is, as a document which was given you by the Office of the President and which will serve you in your cross-examination today. Of course, needless to say, the probative value accorded to this document will be determined by the Chamber in due time. Naturally, with regard to the weight and probative value of this document, it can be challenged also and will be determined by the Chamber in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could look, please, Mr. Maric, at the original in your language, and we'll place it on the ELMO, it's headed, "The appointment of Darko Kraljevic to the HVO General Staff may lead to the disintegration of the defence organisation in Vitez and to the fall of Vitez into Muslim hands," and the report, like the covering letter, is dated the 18th of February, 1994. Now, it then says as follows: "We found out from reliable sources that a meeting will be held today, the 18th of February, in which the status of Darko Kraljevic will be discussed. At that meeting Darko Kraljevic will be given the rank of HVO Colonel and appointed to the HVO General Staff." Were you aware of Darko Kraljevic becoming, or indeed hoping to become, an HVO Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Double hearsay. We have no idea who wrote this report; we have no idea who the reliable source is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, you know well what our position is concerning this issue. It is still the same jurisprudence. The weight and the probative value will be determined by the Judges. Mr. Maric, did you hear any talk about this or not? And we shall, of course, appreciate at a later stage the weight we should accord to your statement. So the question that is asked of you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this event at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next paragraph begins in this way: "According to a reliable source, Darko Kraljevic, with the help of Dario Kordic and Ignac Kostroman, intends to use this appointment to the HVO General Staff to destroy Colonel Blaskic. There has been a concealed and very bitter conflict between Dario Kordic and Kostroman with the presidents of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca HVO in Central Bosnia for quite some time." Now, pausing there and taking it in reverse order, had there been an issue in respect of which the presidents of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca HVOs had been allies?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, objection. Double hearsay. I apologise for interrupting, but I want to ensure we create a clear record here for future purposes. Once again, double hearsay. We don't know who wrote this report. That person, an unidentified, anonymous author, is quoting an allegedly reliable source who, again, we have no idea as to the identity of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, we shall ask you not to interrupt us again on this issue. You have had the opportunity to explain your position; it is in the transcript and it is on record. The position of the Chamber is once again the same. We shall hear what the witness tells us. As for the hearsay, as we have done before, we shall act in the same way and we shall decide what weight and what value to accord to what is said. Mr. Maric, will you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for this document, I am not familiar with it at all. I do not know what was discussed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, and it relates to the contents of the document but it comes from your memory, is this: Was there an issue in this time, leading up to February 1994, where the presidents of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, and the Busovaca HVOs were allies, an issue where you were working together to achieve an objective?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer when I simply cannot remember when the meeting was, where it was. I simply haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, think back. You've come here and given us a great deal of detail, as you told us, from your memory which, you say, required no help from documents. Was there an issue where you four HVO presidents were either associated with, it's not entirely clear, or alternatively against Kordic and Kostroman on an issue that related, it would appear, to Kraljevic? Was there such an issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat once again: We were never against Kordic or anyone, and so I cannot speak about something that is not true. I cannot talk about this document that I know nothing about. This is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you against Blaskic, all of you, at some stage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could one be against a man fighting for his people?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then I'm not going to go through the rest of it line by line, not only because of the lateness of the hour but for other reasons, but just tell me -- remember what I asked you earlier, think back, please -- Mr. Kordic, did he, as time went by, assume more military authority, ever more military authority?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I affirm to this day, that Kordic was a politician not a soldier. He was always a politician and he never aspired to run the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to take that document any further with this witness because we've passed the passage where he's specifically identified, and that's what I wanted his answers on. I'm in this position: There's a great deal more I would have asked if time had been unlimited, and I certainly haven't joined issue with this witness on all the topics that he gave evidence on yesterday and to which we would wish to ask questions. However, I am content to end my cross-examination on the basis that the witness is going home this weekend. But if there's an application, for example, to have his re-examination taken on Monday so that he's going to be here in any event, well, then I'd ask for a little more time on Monday to deal with some of the central issues that I would have been dealing with in any event if I hadn't been constrained by time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so many subjects were brought up and I also would have a number of questions, but I know that Mr. Maric has to go home. So perhaps I could manage to finish it all in less than ten minutes, or perhaps ten minutes. I would not go into all the subjects. If you give me ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We shall begin from the end, Mr. Maric. From this document, and you heard what we think about it, the gist of what you were asked now is that there was a very serious fallout between the presidents of the HVO, that is, the civilian government in Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca and therefore you personally on the one hand, and Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Ignac Kostroman on the other, because of the whole situation in the Lasva Valley. Did that ever really happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat once again: There was never any conflict between the civilian side of the HVO and the military side of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But this also speaks of a conflict with Mr. Kordic personally and Mr. Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no, not ever with the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: To conclude, so this is a false claim in this document.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is false because I know that there never was any conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Document 861 is the certificate with three signatures; the brigade commander, Dusko Grubesic, then you in the centre as the prime minister, and the vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Dario Kordic. Would you agree with me that this document shows best this distribution of power because it is signed by the military commander, a representative of the civilian government, that is, you, and Mr. Dario Kordic as the vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, as the politician?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. This document about Kuber, the attack on Kuber, Colonel Blaskic's order of the 16th of April, 1993, you say this order does not interfere with what you say, that the battle on Kuber began on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battle on Kuber began on the 15th, and the Muslim forces were advancing on the territory of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without wasting time, I should like to draw your attention to item 1 in this document, Z684, where it says that the Muslim forces are advancing with a view to taking Kuber in full which does not exclude any previous fighting. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that you attended a meeting in Croatia with President Tudjman in March 1993. I had several questions but there is no time for that, so only one question. Mr. Kordic was not at that meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Some reports, some milinfosums, of the British Battalion were read here about events on the 20th, that is, 21st of January, 1991 in Busovaca. You were asked by the Prosecutor a very long question and you answered it in part but I don't think that you answered all parts of that question. My question is as follows: On those days, the 20th, 21st, 22nd, 23rd of January, 1993, did the authorities in Busovaca organise any attack on Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities never organised an attack on the Muslims. Never. I swear by my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So there wasn't a plan of attack.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Incidentally, you were asked by the Prosecutor if you had talked to the investigators of this Tribunal. Tell us, Mr. Maric, did the investigators of The Hague Tribunal ever invite you, as the president of the HVO at that time, to have any meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never invited to any meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So are you telling the Court that you, as the president of the government in those years, 1992/1993, that is, 1994, nobody ever asked you with a view to talk, with a view to establish -- to finding facts to establish the situation in Busovaca in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never invited to discuss these events in 1992, 1993, 1994. Nobody, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. There were two or three questions which came down to your knowledge about an alleged fallout between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that there has been ever any fallout between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not want to waste any more time by showing the witness D52/1. It's a document that we adduced, and I should like merely to draw attention to item 4 of this document, showing that Colonel Blaskic is suggesting that Mr. Kordic, as the president of the HZ HB, should attend some talks in Sarajevo. That is all that I wanted to draw the attention of the Court to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You already said something about Mr. Kordic's photograph. Did you ever see Mr. Kordic with any rifle or any weapons for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him with a rifle or a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You were shown document Z120. It is an order, I don't know if you remember, about sending a unit to Rasni Do [phoen], a unit of 100 men or something, and it is signed by the vice-president of the HVO, Dario Kordic, and the secretary of the HVO, Ignac Kostroman. Did they have any military responsibilities, the two gentlemen who have signed here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is the 1st of June, 1992; Z120 bears that date. That is the document. Do you know if the commander before Colonel Blaskic was Tole who was captured by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree that this document was issued before Colonel Blaskic became the commander of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is, the 1st of June, 1991, it is the period of time when the power was not yet divided that you told us about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. A document has very often come up here in this case, Z76.1, and that is the delivery list or the shipping order. We have another document, Z78A and B, and this document, Mr. Kordic signed, but that is in the capacity that you already saw, the secretary of the secretariat for the People's Defence. We saw it, but perhaps, sir, you can enlighten us. Pursuant to the order of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an indication of the need to urgently remove, that is, dislocate finished products from the weapons factory, Bratstvo, in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you remember if at that time everything possible was done to take as many weapons from the JNA as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, because a year and a half before that, the weapons that were held by the Territorial Defence of Busovaca, that is, in all municipalities, all these weapons were withdrawn and stood in the barracks; that is, it was taken away. In point of fact, it was taken away from the TO, which could manage those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We have to be mindful of the time, so will you please keep your answers as short as possible. Did the Busovaca HVO ever have at its disposal those sophisticated means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you a set of Official Gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina reporting that these were the only lawful laws, that is, that the only valid laws were the ones carried by that Official Gazette. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these sets of the Official Gazette never reached the municipality of Busovaca. These, I would have certainly had them in my hands as the mayor of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Then let us try to explain it to the Court as follows: After the conclusion of the Dayton Accords, did the Dayton Accords accept as valid all three types of laws; that is, laws adopted by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, laws adopted by the Croat Community, that is, Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the laws passed by the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Dayton and Washington Accords were concluded, all the laws of all the three sides became valid, until such time -- until such -- until the beginning of the functioning of the parliament. Now it is adopting official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But since not all the documents have been adopted as yet for Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are still some laws of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna which are still in effect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there are still some of these laws which are still in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, one question to do with the legal, that is, legitimate power. You explained to us why you thought that the Croats had legitimate right to introduce their authority. Just one sentence. Do you agree with me that the lawful and legitimate power of the Croat Defence Council, that is, Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, was the counterpart which was recognised by the International Community together with other two counterparts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both at the time of the conclusion of the Dayton Accords and the Washington Agreements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was the basis for both the Washington and the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it merely goes to confirm the legality and the legitimacy of the power which was set up in the days when the old power had fallen apart?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a few more moments. Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A great deal was said, or rather the Prosecutor characterised it and said Tudjman was sending weapons, and you told us about different ways in which weapons arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I must ask the interpreters also to be patient with us. We shall accord a few more minutes. I suppose they agree. Thank you. Because they also have their union rights. Thank you very so much for being so cooperative.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could Mr. Naumovski please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can confirm that I will finish in five minutes. But on the other hand, I'm being warned that I have to slow down, so it is difficult to both be slow and finish it. But thank you very much. I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the collection of weapons took different forms; it was both taken away from the JNA, purchased, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After April 1993, that is, after this second conflict began, and then it lasted that whole year, that is, until the next spring, are you aware that in Croatia a large number of Muslim refugees from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were accommodated in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. There were over 200.000 who were accommodated in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you first mentioned it, the transcript recorded 500 expelled persons. That is why I had to ask you that. Are you aware that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't ask questions about that. It's one of the various topics that I haven't covered. And to put a huge leading question in that form is valueless to the exercise, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is in the record, in the transcript, Your Honours, and that's why I reacted, because there was a figure of 500 mentioned, and that is not realistic, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Are you also aware that in Split, in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, will you please -- I do not remember either 500.000 [as interpreted]. Will you just move on, please. Will you please move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. But let me just finish this. We shall not dwell on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware that throughout the war between Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had its logistical and military centers in Split and Zagreb, in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm saying, are you aware that for the duration of the war between the Muslims and between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had its logistical centers in Split and in Zagreb in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And as for the speech on the 16th of January, 1992, and what Mr. Kostroman had said, you already explained it to the Prosecutor. My only question is: You said that you disagreed with that political option?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on the table there were quite a number of political options until the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course there were all sorts of options.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In your conversations with President Tudjman, was there ever any mention about the violent takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was never brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There was another question, and the Prosecutor asked who was the politician who managed to run the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I shall ask you: Did any politician in Bosnia-Herzegovina ever run the army in which the war --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was there any politician who ran, who led the army, who headed the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not coming back to that point. The witness has already spoken to us about Mr. Boban, his role, about the politicians and the military. I do not think we have to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I won't, Your Honour. No, I will not do that. Perhaps my final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At the time when the HVO government in Busovaca was set up in May 1992, was there a central government, central authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina which could organise life in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really would have very many questions, but I am fully aware of the time, so I should like to thank you for the patience and to thank Mr. Maric for his answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Naumovski. Mr. Kovacic, we have forgotten you. Do you -- I still have to ask you: Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Very well. Mr. Maric, you have finished giving your evidence before the International Criminal Tribunal. Thank you very much for coming here to testify before the International Criminal Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session is adjourned and we shall resume -- Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that we shall be resuming at half past 9.00 with Judge May and Judge Robinson, as it has been announced to you. As for me, I shall be on another case. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm simply going to ask, through the Court, whether we could have the summaries for next week's witness, who of course musn't be mentioned, immediately, because they are in each case indicated as substantial witnesses, and the difficulties of preparing at short notice are very great. And indeed the second thing I would ask is that we can have a list of witnesses that extends beyond next week, for I don't think we've got one at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait. Could the witness please go. I believe we should allow the witness to leave. Usher, will you please escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witnesses for next week are beginning to arrive today, and we will provide the Court and the Prosecution -- if the Court still wants the summaries, if it feels that they're at all useful, we're more than happy to continue the exercise. I'm sure the Court can appreciate that it's an extremely substantial exercise putting these documents together, but we're happy to continue to do that and we will provide them to the Prosecution in a timely fashion as soon as they're signed. We anticipate that the first one should be available to be delivered to the Prosecution first thing tomorrow morning, maybe 10.00 or 11.00, and the other three should be available, once they've been prepared, certainly by the -- before the beginning of the first session on Monday. So that way the Prosecution should have them all. Insofar as a batting order is concerned, we will give the Prosecution a batting order for the week of the 20th. We haven't made final decisions regarding those witnesses yet, but we'll alert them before the end of next week and try to give them a batting order for the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will Mr. Sayers slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the translators. We'll give a batting order for two weeks to the Prosecution sometime towards the end of next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the fortnight list, for a list, we agreed. We discussed. We do, yes; we agree with you. As for the summaries, that is, the text which concerns the examination-in-chief of witnesses, we believe the Chamber considers them very useful, because they help us to prepare, to follow easier. I cannot, of course, encourage you to continue, because this is a serious work. But, Mr. Nice, are you satisfied with what has just been proposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the provisions of summaries, thank you very much. As to the provision of a witness list, I think the provision of a list only in the middle of next week is really very late. I think, by and large, the minimum that the Rule imposed right at the beginning of the case required was that there should be a notice the next two weeks of witnesses. And really we should have, at any given time, a notice of the next two weeks to come. Of course I'm not unsympathetic to difficulties in the way of getting witnesses here, and of course decisions made will be contingent upon the performance of earlier witnesses. I understand that. Nevertheless, I would respectfully invite the Court to make it really the case that there's always a minimum of two weeks of -- two working weeks of witnesses available for us to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, there will be. The week of June 12th, I believe, is -- there's no court that week. So if we give the Prosecution a list of witnesses for the next two weeks, it's going to be the week of the 20th and the week of the 27th. They can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I was going to say. Any matter as of the next week, yes, there will be one week to prepare. But it doesn't prevent you, of course, to give them really as they come so that the Prosecution could be prepared. So tomorrow you will have the summary for the witnesses who will be here on Monday, and I suppose that you will have them 24 hours in the advance for the witnesses who will follow. Thank you. This session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: at 4.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 5th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
